---
title: "Five weeks of study: work, outputs, and review"
---

The course is organised as 25 study units. Each combines explanation, guided
work, independent transfer, and a result you can save, explain, and regenerate.
The independent tasks are part of the course, not optional advanced extensions.
They gradually remove prompts so that a later laboratory dataset is manageable.

## Planning a full study week

The planning estimate is **35 hours of structured study plus 5 flexible hours
per week**, about 200 learner hours over five weeks. These are not contact
hours or a requirement to keep working after a task is securely understood.
They include reading, demonstrations, active practicals, writing, troubleshooting,
and independent review. Actual timing will be checked with beginners; previous
experience and installation problems can change it substantially. The teaching
team supplies the contact timetable separately. Examination design is outside
these materials.

| Activity on a typical study day | Planning allowance | Evidence of work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lecture, prediction pauses, and teacher demonstrations | 1 hour | Predictions and a short explanation of the worked example |
| Guided practical and checking results | 2 hours | Saved commands/code, checked numerical or file results |
| Extended practical and independent transfer | 2 hours | New outputs from a changed question, file, or dataset |
| Interpretation, report writing, and fresh-session recovery | 1 hour | A readable conclusion and a reproducible saved result |
| Supported catch-up or further rehearsal of that day's tasks | 1 hour | Corrected work and a record of an issue resolved |

Across five days this gives 35 hours. Use the remaining **5 flexible hours each
week** for the weekly quiz and explanation review, unfinished practical work,
help sessions, or repeating the workflow without looking at the worked example.
Breaks are additional; this table does not prescribe seven uninterrupted hours
at a screen. A substantial independent report may span more than one session.

The allowances are a shared daily budget, not upper bounds to add together.
If an extended/transfer block takes three hours, use the protected catch-up
hour for that work rather than adding another hour to the day. A context choice
replaces its alternative; it does not double that task. Bring persistent timing
problems to the teaching team so the plan can be adjusted from actual experience.

## What makes the second half of a practical different?

The first examples show how to perform a task. The **Extended practical** asks
you to trace consequences, diagnose a plausible mistake, or work through a
larger case. **Independent transfer** changes the question or input and gives
fewer prompts. You should choose and explain operations already taught, rather
than reproduce a screenshot by changing only the title.

Use hints when stuck, but record what changed and why. The target is being able
to find and regenerate work after closing the applications. A calculation typed
once in a console is not the final output of a data-analysis task.

## Weekly sequence and checkpoints

| Week | Main work | Checkpoint before moving on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 — Files and computers | Save/find/reopen; folder trees; memory/storage/processes; terminal navigation; archives; text search; deliberate transfer and recovery | Identify the same folder in graphical and terminal views, inspect a new archive, preserve originals, and package findings |
| 2 — R and reports | Objects/vectors; table import and units; calculations; plots; R Markdown; apply the workflow to another small table | Run saved code from the top and render a report whose objects all come from its source |
| 3 — Reliable measurements | Evidence-based cleaning; missingness; mean/variance/SD; grouped observations; independent units; sampling uncertainty | Explain counts and units, distinguish spread from uncertainty, and produce a descriptive report with visible observations |
| 4 — Comparisons and lines | Independent and paired comparisons; interpretation of effects/intervals/p-values; calibration and range checks; observational line fits | Explain the design and comparison direction; apply the same simple method to fresh measurements and report its limits |
| 5 — Reproduce and transfer | Local/remote project workflow; representations; a substantial integrated study; fresh data; peer reproduction; debugging and consolidation | Supply source/input/output together, render from another location, and explain an independent transfer result |

All chemistry contexts give their quantities, units, relationships, and meaning
of terms. You do not need to have taken a chemistry course to know what to
compute. Where an organic or biological context is offered as a choice, work
through the chosen route in depth; you are not expected to complete duplicate
reports for every context.

## A study log that helps you learn

Keep a short daily note in `reports/study-log.txt`. Record the output you saved,
one result you checked, one decision you can explain, and one question remaining.
Examples: “the count includes a header”, “these two readings belong to one plant”,
or “the report depended on an object only in the console”. This is a learning
record, not a grading scheme.

If a task runs much longer than planned, bring the exact error and the last
successful step to a support session. If you finish quickly, try the transfer
without the hints, explain it to a peer, or reproduce a previous result from its
raw input. Do not fill spare time by inventing additional statistical methods.
